problem: Learning-based topological navigation methods such as SPTM and ViNG build static graphs from all collected trajectory images. The learned connectivity model inevitably produces spurious edges (false positives) and missing edges (false negatives), and these cause plan failures that the graph never corrects. The graphs are also dense, ignore the controller's real capability, and miss loop closures between nodes that are spatially close but temporally far apart; ViNG additionally needs about 40 h of real-world data.
motivation: Image-goal topological navigation is attractive because goals are intuitive images and no expert SLAM map-building is needed, while a local controller only has to traverse short edges. However, the graph quality determines success. The authors observe that an agent's own traversal experience can be used to verify and repair the graph continually (prune bad edges, add missing nodes), and that a sim-pretrained model can be cheaply fine-tuned with only the trajectory used to build the graph.
key_idea: Use one CNN that jointly predicts reachability and relative SE(2) waypoint between two RGB-D images to (a) build a sparse graph by PRM/RRT-style sampling over sensor data with merge/connect thresholds, (b) localize and drive a waypoint controller, and (c) continually maintain the graph via Bayesian edge-connectivity and edge-weight updates plus on-demand node addition during lifelong operation.
insight: Sparse, controller-aware graphs built by sampling (merging near-duplicate observations and connecting only locally traversable pairs) give both higher success and far fewer nodes and edges than the all-images graphs of SPTM and ViNG after fine-tuning (Fig. nav_performance; only shown in figures). Treating edges as uncertain beliefs updated from experience matters most. In simulation, lifelong maintenance first reduces the edge count by pruning spurious cross-wall edges and then adds a few useful nodes, and success rises with more queries. In the real world, 30 maintenance queries raise success from 4/20 to 13/20 (apartment) and 4/20 to 14/20 (lab). Defining reachability analytically (visual overlap, path-length ratio, visibility, distance/yaw limits) allows i.i.d. sim data. Using odometry plus a temporal window H as proxy labels allows cheap target-domain fine-tuning.
method: Reachability + waypoint model: CNN f(o_i,o_j) on two 96x72 RGB-D images outputs a reachability score r̂ and relative waypoint [dx,dy,dθ]. It is trained with BCE for reachability plus L2 position loss and sin/cos L1 rotation loss, with the waypoint losses applied only to reachable pairs (weights α, β).

Automated dataset creation: in simulation, i.i.d. image pairs are labeled reachable if visual overlap > L_min (from depth), shortest-path/Euclidean ratio < R_max, the target is visible in the source image, distance < E_max and yaw < Θ_max (Dubins-style controller assumption; 288k pairs from 10 iGibson scenes). Fine-tuning in the target environment uses the graph-building trajectory with odometry as pose labels, and pairs within H time steps count as reachable.

Sampling-based graph building: starting from a random node, trajectory images are drawn in random order. isMergeable (distance < D_m) discards redundant nodes; isConnectable (distance < D_c) adds a node with edges weighted by d(w)=||log T(w)||_F in SE(2). This repeats until no node can be added, and unused images are kept as T'.

Navigation: the agent localizes by nearest predicted distance below D_ℓ (local search over neighbours of the last plan first, then global). Dijkstra plans to the goal node, the first node on the path becomes the subgoal, and a position-based feedback controller (iLQR from PyRobot on the real robot) drives to the predicted waypoint. The agent then relocalizes and repeats; it rotates in place to recover if localization fails.

Edge maintenance: each edge's connectivity is ~Bernoulli(p), initialized from r̂ and updated by a discrete Bayes rule from traversal success (checked with isConnectable(o_d,o_j)); an edge is pruned when p < R_p. Each edge weight is ~Gaussian, initialized from the predicted distance with a validation-set variance, and updated with a Gaussian filter on successful traversals.

Graph expansion: observations that cannot be localized are added as novel nodes. When no path to the goal exists, nodes are sampled from T' into a candidate set until a path is found, and only candidates on the path are kept; the others return to T'. Criteria are loosened (larger D_c, smaller D_m) to handle sharp turns.

setting.backbone: custom CNN reachability/waypoint model (trained from scratch in simulation, fine-tuned per target environment) + graph search (Dijkstra) + position-based feedback controller
setting.training_data: 288,000 simulated RGB-D image pairs from 10 iGibson interactive environments (fully supervised); per-environment fine-tuning on the teleoperated graph-building trajectory with odometry (985 / 1,685 / 1,609 / 2,243 images for Barahona / Bellemeade / Akiak / Caruthers; 3-4 loops in real-world spaces)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (96x72); goal given as an RGB-D image; odometry used only for fine-tuning labels
setting.action_space: predicted relative waypoints (dx, dy, dθ) executed by a position-based feedback controller (iLQR via PyRobot on the real robot)
setting.privileged: pre-exploration: teleoperated trajectory (3-4 loops) of the test environment is collected to build the graph and fine-tune the model; goal images are chosen from graph locations; no GT pose/map at navigation time

numbers_note: All simulation results are shown only in figures (Fig. nav_performance: success rate and graph size vs SPTM/ViNG before and after fine-tuning; Fig. lifelong_results: SR, #nodes and #edges vs number of queries). They cover four unseen Gibson scenes (Barahona, Bellemeade, Akiak, Caruthers) with 500 episodes each and 3 seeds, and no numeric values are printed. The only table with numbers is the real-world Table II, printed as successes/20; SR values here are exact conversions of those fractions.
results: In four unseen Gibson scenes, the fine-tuned model with sampling-based graphs achieves consistently higher image-goal navigation success than SPTM and ViNG (the latter given 500k vs 288k training points). It also uses significantly fewer nodes and edges and gains more from fine-tuning, but the numbers appear only in figures. Lifelong graph maintenance first prunes spurious edges and then adds a few nodes, and success improves with more queries while graph size stays roughly flat. On a real LoCoBot, 30 maintenance queries raise success from 4/20 to 13/20 in an apartment and from 4/20 to 14/20 in a university lab, more than a 3x increase.
limitations: Fine-tuning requires piloted/teleoperated trajectories with odometry of the target environment (pre-exploration); it cannot use unordered images or images from other sources such as a phone.
Assumes a static environment; non-stationary scenes are not handled.

Evaluation is small-scale and custom: 4 Gibson scenes with results only in figures, 20-episode real-world tests, and several hand-tuned thresholds (D_m, D_c, D_ℓ, R_p). Comparison is only to SPTM and ViNG (SPTM modified with a pose estimator and the same controller).
